title: The man-eating king
hookLine: a prince keeps his word to return to a captor, and changes him (Jataka 537)

cards: It starts with a promise to a stranger. A traveling brahmin arrives with verses to teach, and Prince Sutasoma tells him: wait here, I'll hear them when I come back from my bath. He never makes it back.
On the road, a man who eats people snatches him and carries him into the forest. Now the prince has a promise he can't keep, and a captor with no reason to let him go.

teach.b: The captor, the Jataka says, was once a king who acquired a taste for human flesh, was driven from his kingdom, and now lives in the forest as a man-eater.
Carried off, Sutasoma weeps, and the man-eater mocks him for fearing death. That's not why I'm crying, the prince says. I made a promise to a brahmin and left it unkept.
Let me go, and I'll keep it, and I'll come back. The man-eater lets him go, sure he'll never see him again. Sutasoma goes home, hears the verses, rewards the brahmin.
His family begs him to stay.
He goes back anyway, alone, to the man who plans to eat him. The man-eater is stunned. Who walks back to his own death to keep a word?
He asks to hear the verses, and they're about the worth of keeping company with good people. He offers the prince a gift for each one.
Among the gifts Sutasoma asks for: give up eating human flesh, and set your captives free. The man-eater agrees, and the captives go home.
Nothing here is forced. No army, no trick. The captor is changed by watching someone keep a promise that cost him everything.
Tradition reads it as a picture of sacca, truthfulness, one of the ten perfections.

how: Buddhist teachers tell the Sutasoma story as an example of truthfulness (sacca), one of the ten perfections; keeping one's word is part of right speech in everyday practice.

o: a promise made to a god

games.q: who did what in Sutasoma's story: tap the pairs.
p: the prince who promised to return
let him go, sure he'd never return

s: the prince wept because he feared death
he wept over a promise to the brahmin he hadn't kept.
the man-eater was defeated by an army
nothing was forced; he was changed by a kept promise and the verses.
the verses praise keeping company with good people
the man-eater asks to hear them, and offers a gift for each.

games.q: you're Sutasoma. you've kept your promise to the brahmin. your family begs you not to go back to the man-eater. what do you do?
o: stay home; a promise to a man-eater doesn't count.
go back alone, as you said you would.
go back with soldiers and end the threat.
games.why: he goes back alone, and the man-eater, stunned that anyone would, asks to hear the verses and is changed.

practice: Bring to mind something you said you'd do that's still open: a call, a favor, a 'let me get back to you.' Picture actually doing it, where you'll be and what you'll say, and let any reluctance be there without fighting it while you hold the picture of the promise kept.

wordCard.voice: Sacca. Truth, truthfulness: the perfection behind the man-eating king who let Prince Sutasoma go, never expecting him back, and was changed when he returned. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali sacca: truth, and truthfulness, the perfection Sutasoma's kept word shows.

carryVoice: Your line: he came back. A kept word did what a sword couldn't. That's day eight hundred thirty-nine.
